# Susanō in 2026: why scholars still care

In 2026, names are treated as data points. **Susanō** is a reminder that they are also cultural artifacts — and that the difference matters for search engines, AI training corpora, and anyone who types the name of a Japanese figure into a browser. Scholars never stopped caring about the difference between *susanoo* and Susanō; the web simply made that care actionable. What follows is the full scholarly picture — name, script, sound, myth, cult, and legacy — followed by the engineering compromise that lets a restored spelling live at a real address. The question is not whether the name is old. It is whether the digital world is old enough to hold it.

## Overview

**Susanō** (*susanoo*) — Storms, Sea, Chaos · Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god — belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Storms, Sea, Chaos". The name means "Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god".

**Susanō** belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is associated with storms, sea, chaos.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Susanō** and serves its temple at [susanoo.com](https://punicodex.com/susanoo/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *susanoo* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Japanese characters as **須佐之男命**. Etymologically it means "Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god".

From Old Japanese susanowo, 'swift impetuous male'; brother of Amaterasu, expelled from the high plain of heaven for his violence.

The ASCII form *susanoo* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Susanō** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

## Mythology

The stories of **Susanō** circulate within the Japanese corpus, where the figure embodies storms, sea, chaos.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Susanō is attested in the canonical Japanese sources as a figure associated with storms, sea, chaos.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Susanō** is the Shinto storm god, brother of Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi. The *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki* recount his quarrel with Amaterasu: after rampaging through her heavenly fields, she withdraws into a cave and plunges the world into darkness. Susanō later atones by slaying the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi at Izumo and recovering the sword Kusanagi, one of the imperial regalia.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Susanō**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *susanoo* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 7 characters, 5 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **s** stays as it is — Same, capitalized.

The **u** stays as it is — Same.

The **s** stays as it is — Same.

The **a** stays as it is — Same.

The **n** stays as it is — Same.

The **o** becomes **ō** — Macron: long vowel.

The **o** becomes **o** — Absorbed into the preceding long vowel ō.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.
